clinicalPearls: Brain injury in the term or near-term newborn resulting from a perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic insult
Severity is graded clinically (for example by the Sarnat stages) from mild irritability to severe coma with absent reflexes
Features include altered tone and consciousness, poor feeding, abnormal primitive reflexes and seizures
Therapeutic hypothermia started within the first hours improves outcomes in moderate to severe cases meeting criteria
It is important to exclude and treat other causes of neonatal encephalopathy such as infection, metabolic disease and stroke
MRI and amplitude-integrated or standard EEG help characterise injury and prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy follows an interruption of oxygen delivery and blood flow to the brain around the time of birth. The initial insult causes primary energy failure with cell depolarisation, and after partial recovery a delayed secondary energy failure ensues over hours, driven by excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation and apoptosis, which extends the injury. This latent interval is the rationale for therapeutic hypothermia, which slows the injurious cascade. Patterns of injury depend on the severity and duration of the insult and on regional vulnerability of the immature brain.
additionalInvestigations: Cord and early blood gases and assessment of the perinatal history
Amplitude-integrated or conventional EEG for background activity and seizures
MRI of the brain to define injury pattern and prognosis
Investigations to exclude infection and metabolic causes
redFlags: Moderate to severe encephalopathy meeting cooling criteria (time-critical)
Deep or extensive injury on MRI
reference.prognosis: Mild encephalopathy often has a good outcome, whereas moderate to severe disease carries significant risk of death or long-term disability including cerebral palsy, epilepsy and cognitive impairment; therapeutic hypothermia improves survival free of disability.
pitfalls: Missing the narrow window for therapeutic hypothermia
Attributing all neonatal encephalopathy to hypoxia-ischaemia without excluding mimics
Overlooking subclinical seizures detectable on EEG
management: Initiate therapeutic hypothermia (whole-body or selective head cooling) within the first hours of life for moderate to severe encephalopathy meeting cooling criteria, maintaining controlled hypothermia before slow rewarming
Provide meticulous neonatal intensive care, maintaining normal oxygenation, ventilation, glucose and blood pressure and avoiding hyperoxia, hypocapnia and hyperthermia which worsen injury
Treat clinical and subclinical seizures with antiseizure medication (phenobarbital first-line) under amplitude-integrated and conventional EEG guidance
Recognise and manage multi-organ dysfunction affecting the kidneys, liver, heart, gut and coagulation with cautious fluid balance and organ support
Exclude and treat mimics of neonatal encephalopathy including infection, inborn errors of metabolism and perinatal stroke
Characterise injury and prognosis with brain MRI and EEG, and counsel the family clearly
Arrange structured neurodevelopmental follow-up and early intervention within a neonatology and paediatric neurology service
